topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Understanding quadrilaterals
topic.scope: polygons, angle sum, kinds of quadrilaterals, properties of parallelogram, rhombus, rectangle, square, mid-point theorem

nodes.name: Mid-point theorem
external_prereqs: ratio and half of a length

nodes.name: Polygon is a closed figure of line segments
Regular polygon: equal sides and equal angles
Interior angle sum of n-gon is (n-2)×180°
Exterior angles of any convex polygon sum to 360°
Each angle of a regular n-gon
Trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides (NCERT)
Kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides
Hierarchy: square, rectangle, rhombus are parallelograms
Opposite sides and angles of a parallelogram are equal
Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary
Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
Square diagonals are equal and perpendicular bisectors
Segment joining midpoints is parallel to third side and half of it
Converse: line through midpoint parallel to a side bisects the other side

misconceptions.statement: A polygon with an angle larger than 180° is not a proper polygon.
misconceptions.why: Students' prototypes of polygons are only convex shapes like regular pentagons.
misconceptions.fix: A concave polygon has at least one interior angle more than 180° and is still a polygon.

probe.question: Is an arrowhead-shaped four-sided closed figure a polygon?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is not a polygon because it is dented.

misconceptions.root_belief: only typical-looking examples count as the category
misconceptions.source_hint: research on geometric prototype images in concept formation

misconceptions.statement: A polygon with all sides equal is always regular.
misconceptions.why: Students remember one condition and forget the angle condition, as in a square.
misconceptions.fix: A regular polygon needs both equal sides and equal angles; a rhombus has equal sides but unequal angles.

probe.question: Is a rhombus that is not a square a regular polygon?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because all its sides are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: one property is enough to define a category
misconceptions.source_hint: research on van Hiele levels and property-based definitions

misconceptions.statement: The interior angle sum of a polygon is always 360°.
misconceptions.why: Students generalise from quadrilaterals and from the exterior angle sum.
misconceptions.fix: The interior angle sum is (n-2)×180°, so it grows with the number of sides; only exterior angles always total 360°.

probe.question: What is the sum of interior angles of a hexagon?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The angle sum of an n-sided polygon is (n-1)×180° or n×180°.
misconceptions.why: Students misremember the formula without knowing it comes from dividing into n-2 triangles.
misconceptions.fix: Drawing diagonals from one vertex makes n-2 triangles, so the sum is (n-2)×180°.

probe.question: Find the interior angle sum of a pentagon.

misconceptions.root_belief: memorised formulas need no reason

misconceptions.statement: A polygon with more sides has a larger sum of exterior angles.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over the idea that interior angle sum grows with sides.
misconceptions.fix: The exterior angles of any convex polygon add to 360°, one full turn, whatever the number of sides.

probe.question: What is the sum of the exterior angles (one at each vertex) of a decagon?

misconceptions.root_belief: more parts means a bigger total

misconceptions.statement: An exterior angle is the same as the interior angle at that vertex.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the two words and ignore that they form a linear pair.
misconceptions.fix: An exterior angle and the interior angle at the same vertex are a linear pair, adding to 180°.

probe.question: A polygon's interior angle is 110°. What is the exterior angle there?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding words mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Each angle of a regular polygon is 360° divided by the number of sides.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the exterior angle formula with the interior angle formula.
misconceptions.fix: 360°/n gives each exterior angle; each interior angle is (n-2)×180°/n, or 180° minus the exterior angle.

probe.question: Find each interior angle of a regular hexagon.

misconceptions.root_belief: a formula works for any similar quantity

misconceptions.statement: A rhombus is the same as a square, and a square drawn tilted is a rhombus but not a square.
misconceptions.why: Orientation changes how a shape looks, and students tie names to the upright picture.
misconceptions.fix: A shape's name depends on its sides and angles, not on its orientation; a rhombus with 90° angles is a square.

probe.question: A square is rotated by 45°. Is it still a square?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is now a diamond or rhombus only.

misconceptions.root_belief: appearance in one position defines the shape
misconceptions.source_hint: research on orientation effects in shape recognition by children

misconceptions.statement: A square is not a rectangle, and a rectangle is not a parallelogram.
misconceptions.why: Students treat shape names as separate exclusive boxes, learnt from pictures.
misconceptions.fix: Every square is a rectangle and a rhombus, and every rectangle is a parallelogram, because they meet the parallelogram's conditions.

probe.question: Is every rectangle a parallelogram?

misconceptions.root_belief: categories never overlap or include each other
misconceptions.source_hint: research on class inclusion of quadrilaterals (van Hiele, de Villiers)

misconceptions.statement: A parallelogram must have unequal adjacent sides and slanted angles, so a rectangle's properties don't apply to it.
misconceptions.why: The typical drawn parallelogram is a slanted shape with no right angles.
misconceptions.fix: Properties of a parallelogram apply to rectangles, rhombuses and squares too, since these are special parallelograms.

probe.question: Do the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other?
probe.wrong_answer: No, that is only a parallelogram property.

misconceptions.root_belief: the usual example shows all that the category is

misconceptions.statement: A trapezium can have two pairs of parallel sides.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up trapezium with parallelogram, or use a definition from other textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: In NCERT, a trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides; a figure with two pairs is a parallelogram.

probe.question: How many pairs of parallel sides does a trapezium have, as defined in NCERT?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A kite has opposite sides equal, like a parallelogram.
misconceptions.why: Students merge the idea of equal sides with parallelogram's opposite sides.
misconceptions.fix: A kite has two pairs of equal adjacent sides; its opposite sides are usually unequal.

probe.question: In kite ABCD, AB = AD and CB = CD. Is AB = CD always?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, opposite sides of a kite are equal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one shape works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The four angles of a quadrilateral add up to 180° because a triangle's do.
misconceptions.why: Students carry the triangle sum onto any figure.
misconceptions.fix: A quadrilateral splits into two triangles by a diagonal, so its angles add to 2×180° = 360°.

probe.question: Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90°, 80°, 70°. Find the fourth.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: In a parallelogram, all four angles are equal.
misconceptions.why: Students blend rectangle's property with parallelogram's and recall 'opposite angles equal' loosely.
misconceptions.fix: Only opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal; adjacent angles are supplementary and differ unless it is a rectangle.

probe.question: One angle of a parallelogram is 70°. What is the angle next to it?

misconceptions.root_belief: all members share the same value

misconceptions.statement: Adjacent angles in a parallelogram add up to 360°.
misconceptions.why: Students recall that the quadrilateral's angles total 360° and misapply it to a pair.
misconceptions.fix: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram lie between parallel lines, so they are co-interior and add to 180°.

probe.question: If one angle of a parallelogram is 65°, find the adjacent angle.

misconceptions.root_belief: a total applies to any part of the whole

misconceptions.statement: The diagonals of a parallelogram are equal in length.
misconceptions.why: Students recall equal diagonals from rectangles and squares and assume it is true for all.
misconceptions.fix: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other but are equal only when it is a rectangle.

probe.question: A parallelogram has one diagonal 8 cm. What is the other?

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case property holds for the general class
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about quadrilateral properties and definitions

misconceptions.statement: Bisecting diagonals mean the diagonals cut each other at right angles.
misconceptions.why: Students merge the words bisect and perpendicular from the rhombus.
misconceptions.fix: Bisect means cut into two equal halves; the diagonals meet at 90° only in a rhombus or a square.

probe.question: Diagonals of a parallelogram meet at O. Is angle AOB always 90°?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they bisect each other.

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding words mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: The diagonals of a rhombus are equal in length.
misconceptions.why: Students think a rhombus is like a square, where the diagonals are equal.
misconceptions.fix: The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular bisectors of each other but are equal only if it is a square.

probe.question: A rhombus has one diagonal 6 cm. What is the other?

misconceptions.root_belief: a special case property holds for the general class

misconceptions.statement: The diagonals of a rectangle are perpendicular to each other.
misconceptions.why: Students mix rectangle and rhombus diagonal properties.
misconceptions.fix: The diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, but meet at 90° only if it is a square.

probe.question: Are the diagonals of a 3 cm by 5 cm rectangle perpendicular?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar shapes share the same properties

misconceptions.statement: A quadrilateral with equal diagonals that bisect each other must be a square.
misconceptions.why: Students use too few properties to identify a shape.
misconceptions.fix: Equal diagonals that bisect each other make a rectangle; the diagonals must also be perpendicular for a square.

probe.question: A quadrilateral has equal diagonals that bisect each other. What is it?

misconceptions.root_belief: one property is enough to define a category

misconceptions.statement: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is equal to the third side.
misconceptions.why: Students recall 'parallel and related to third side' but forget the factor one-half.
misconceptions.fix: The segment is parallel to the third side and exactly half of it.

probe.question: In triangle ABC, D and E are midpoints of AB and AC and BC = 10 cm. Find DE.

misconceptions.root_belief: memorised statements need no checking

misconceptions.statement: The mid-point segment is half of whichever side it is drawn next to, even if it joins a midpoint to a non-midpoint.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the half rule without checking both endpoints are midpoints.
misconceptions.fix: The half-length rule holds only when both endpoints are midpoints of two sides of the triangle.

probe.question: D is the midpoint of AB and E is any point on AC, with BC = 8 cm. Is DE always 4 cm?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, DE is half of BC.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule applies without checking its conditions

misconceptions.statement: A line drawn through the midpoint of one side of a triangle always bisects the other side.
misconceptions.why: Students drop the condition that the line must be parallel to the third side.
misconceptions.fix: A line through the midpoint of one side bisects the second side only if it is parallel to the third side.

probe.question: A line through the midpoint of AB meets AC at some point. Is that point the midpoint of AC?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule applies without checking its conditions
